short: The study of how real people's emotions, habits and mental shortcuts lead them to make money decisions that are not perfectly rational.
kid: Sometimes we pick a toy just because our friend picked it, not because it is the best one. Learning why people choose like that is what this is all about.
detail: Behavioural finance combines psychology with economics to explain why investors, managers and markets often depart from the textbook picture of fully rational decision-makers. Classical finance assumes people process all information correctly and act in their own best interest; behavioural finance documents systematic, predictable errors such as loss aversion, overconfidence, anchoring and herding. Its foundations include Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky's prospect theory (1979) and Richard Thaler's work on mental accounting; Kahneman won the economics Nobel in 2002 and Thaler in 2017. It matters because these biases can push prices away from fundamental value, fuel bubbles and crashes, and quietly erode individual returns through panic selling or chasing last year's winners. A common confusion is thinking it claims markets are random or people are foolish; it says the errors follow patterns, so they can be anticipated and guarded against.
example: Say a hypothetical equity fund compounds at 12% a year for 10 years, turning ₹1 lakh into about ₹3.11 lakh. An investor in the same fund who buys after good years and panic-sells after bad ones might earn only 8% a year, ending with about ₹2.16 lakh. The roughly ₹95,000 gap comes from behaviour, not from the fund.

short: A repeated, predictable error in thinking, caused by how the brain handles information, that leads people to judge or decide badly.
kid: Sometimes your eyes play tricks, like a straw looking bent in a glass of water. Your thinking can play tricks too, and it plays the same trick again and again.
detail: A cognitive bias is a systematic departure from logical reasoning that arises from the way people gather, process and remember information. Behavioural finance usually separates cognitive biases from emotional biases: cognitive ones stem from faulty reasoning, memory or information processing, such as anchoring, confirmation bias, the availability heuristic, framing, mental accounting and hindsight bias. Because they are errors of thinking rather than feeling, they can often be reduced with better information, checklists, base rates and education; the CFA curriculum, for example, suggests advisers try to correct cognitive errors but adapt to emotional ones. For investors, these biases show up as judging a stock by an old price, ignoring bad news about a favourite holding, or extrapolating recent trends. A common confusion is treating bias as a sign of low intelligence; experienced fund managers and analysts show the same biases.
example: Say an investor bought shares of a hypothetical ABC Ltd at ₹500 and they now trade at ₹350 after weak results. Fixed on ₹500, she refuses to sell until it gets back there, even though the stock must rise about 42.9% (₹150 / ₹350) just to break even.

short: A decision error driven by feelings such as fear, greed, regret or pride rather than by faulty reasoning or missing information.
kid: When you are scared of the dark, you might hide under the blanket even though nothing is there. Feelings can make us choose things our thinking would not.
detail: An emotional bias is a departure from rational decision-making that comes from feelings, impulses or intuition rather than conscious calculation. Common examples in finance are loss aversion, overconfidence, the endowment effect, regret aversion, status quo bias and weak self-control, along with the swings between fear and greed in volatile markets. The framework used in the CFA curriculum separates them from cognitive biases because they are harder to fix with information alone: showing a frightened investor long-run statistics rarely stops panic selling. Advisers therefore often adapt to them instead, for instance by recommending a more conservative allocation, automating investments through SIPs or agreeing on rules in advance. Emotional biases matter most at market extremes, when fear drives heavy redemptions and greed fuels speculative surges. A common confusion is assuming only beginners are emotional; seasoned traders also feel losses sharply.
example: Say an investor puts ₹2 lakh into an index fund and the market falls 30%, cutting it to ₹1.4 lakh. Panicking, he sells. If the market then recovers 50% from the low, the fund would be back to ₹2.1 lakh, but he has locked in a ₹60,000 loss.

short: Mental shortcuts or rules of thumb people use to make quick decisions without fully working through all the available information.
kid: When you see dark clouds, you grab an umbrella without checking the weather report. That quick guess is usually right, but not always.
detail: Heuristics are simple rules or mental shortcuts the brain uses to make judgments quickly when time, information or attention is limited. Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman described three classic ones in 1974: representativeness, availability, and anchoring and adjustment. Heuristics are not bad in themselves; they save effort and often give reasonable answers, which is why investors use rules such as 'buy what you know' or 'keep 100 minus your age in equity'. The problem is that they produce predictable errors, or biases, in situations they do not fit, such as judging a company from one good quarter or relying on whichever price you happened to see first. When many investors use the same shortcut, prices can move together away from fair value. The key distinction: a heuristic is the shortcut, while a bias is the systematic error that the shortcut can create.
example: The '100 minus age' rule of thumb tells a 25-year-old to keep 75% in equity, so with ₹4 lakh she would put ₹3 lakh in equity and ₹1 lakh in debt. It is quick and often sensible, but it ignores her income stability, goals and personal risk tolerance.

short: The tendency to feel the pain of a loss more strongly than the pleasure of an equal gain, often about twice as strongly.
kid: If you lose one sweet, you feel very sad. If you find one extra sweet, you feel only a little happy. Losing feels bigger than finding.
detail: Loss aversion is the finding, central to Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory, that people weigh losses more heavily than gains of the same size. Experiments typically put the ratio at around 2 to 2.25, so a ₹1,000 loss hurts roughly as much as a ₹2,000 gain pleases. It helps explain why many people refuse fair coin-flip bets, hold losing stocks hoping to break even, favour guaranteed products and keep too much money in low-return savings. In markets, it can intensify sell-offs, and economists such as Shlomo Benartzi and Richard Thaler have used it, combined with frequent portfolio checking, to help explain why equities have historically offered a large premium over safe assets. A common confusion is equating it with risk aversion: risk aversion is disliking uncertainty in general, while loss aversion is a specific lopsidedness around a reference point, often the purchase price.
example: Offered a coin toss that wins ₹1,000 on heads and loses ₹1,000 on tails, most people refuse, even though the expected value is zero. Many accept only when the possible win is raised to around ₹2,000, which implies a loss-aversion ratio of about 2.
formula: Loss aversion coefficient (lambda) = Pain from a loss / Pleasure from an equal-sized gain; estimated at about 2.25 by Tversky and Kahneman (1992)

short: A theory of how people really choose under risk: they judge gains and losses from a starting point and feel losses more than gains.
kid: If you expected two sweets and got three, you are happy. If you expected five and got three, you are sad. It is the same three sweets, but your feeling depends on what you expected.
detail: Prospect theory, published by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky in 1979 and refined as cumulative prospect theory in 1992, describes how people actually decide under risk, in contrast to expected utility theory's account of how a rational person should. It has four key features. Outcomes are judged as gains or losses relative to a reference point, not as total wealth. The value function is concave for gains and convex for losses, so people tend to avoid risk when protecting gains but take risks to escape losses. Losses loom larger than gains, typically by about 2 to 2.25 times. And people overweight small probabilities, which helps explain both lottery tickets and insurance. The theory underpins work on framing, mental accounting and the disposition effect, and contributed to Kahneman's 2002 Nobel prize. A common confusion is reading it as randomness; it predicts systematic patterns.
example: Asked to choose between a sure ₹5,000 gain and a 50% chance of ₹10,000, most people take the sure ₹5,000. Asked to choose between a sure ₹5,000 loss and a 50% chance of losing ₹10,000, most gamble. Within each pair the two options have the same expected value: a ₹5,000 gain in the first, a ₹5,000 loss in the second.
formula: Value function: v(x) = x^alpha for gains (x >= 0) and v(x) = -lambda(-x)^beta for losses (x < 0); Tversky and Kahneman (1992) estimated alpha = beta = 0.88 and lambda = 2.25

short: When investors copy what most others are doing, buying or selling because the crowd is, rather than relying on their own analysis.
kid: When one sheep starts running, all the sheep run, even if none of them saw a wolf. People sometimes follow the crowd the same way.
detail: Herding is the tendency of investors to imitate the trades of a larger group instead of acting on their own information or analysis. It can be partly rational, since the crowd may know something, and professional managers may herd to avoid the career risk of being wrong alone. But when many people follow each other, prices can overshoot fundamental value in both directions, feeding bubbles such as the dot-com boom of the late 1990s and sharp sell-offs when sentiment turns. In India, waves of retail money into hot IPOs or fashionable small-cap themes, often sparked by social-media tips, are frequently described as herding. It can also drain liquidity when everyone rushes for the exit at once. A common confusion is equating herding with momentum investing: momentum is a deliberate, rules-based strategy, while herding is copying others without independent judgement.
example: Say shares of a hypothetical XYZ Ltd trade at ₹100, close to an analyst's estimate of fair value. Social-media buzz pulls in buyers who simply follow others, pushing it to ₹180 within weeks. When the buzz fades and it slides back to ₹110, those who bought at ₹180 are down about 38.9%.

short: The tendency to overrate your own knowledge, skill or ability to predict, which leads to too much trading and too much risk.
kid: A child who has just learned to ride a bike might think she can ride with no hands. Feeling too sure can lead to a fall.
detail: Overconfidence bias is the tendency to overestimate one's knowledge, abilities and the accuracy of one's forecasts. Researchers distinguish overestimation (thinking you are better than you are), overplacement (thinking you are better than others) and overprecision (setting forecast ranges too narrow). In investing it leads to frequent trading, concentrated portfolios, too little diversification and underestimated risk. A well-known study by Brad Barber and Terrance Odean of US brokerage accounts in the 1990s found that the most active traders earned clearly lower net returns than the least active, largely because of trading costs. In India, studies by SEBI, the market regulator, have found that a large majority of individual traders in equity futures and options lose money, yet many keep trading. A common confusion is treating confidence as competence; being sure of a view says nothing about whether it is right.
example: Say two hypothetical investors each start with ₹10 lakh and earn the same 12% gross return in a year, taking each to ₹11.2 lakh. One trades rarely and pays ₹5,000 in costs; the other trades daily and pays ₹70,000 in brokerage, transaction taxes and slippage. The first ends with ₹11.15 lakh, the second with only ₹10.5 lakh.

short: Relying too heavily on the first number you see, such as a past price, and adjusting too little when new information arrives.
kid: If someone first tells you a jar holds 100 marbles, you will guess close to 100 even if it holds far fewer. Your mind stays tied to that first number, like a boat to its anchor.
detail: Anchoring is the tendency to fix on an initial reference value, the anchor, and then adjust too little away from it when forming an estimate. Tversky and Kahneman showed in 1974 that even an obviously random number, such as the result of spinning a wheel, shifted people's estimates. In investing, common anchors are the purchase price, a stock's 52-week high, the IPO price, a round index level or an analyst's old price target. An investor may call a stock cheap because it is 40% below its peak, without asking whether the business has changed. Analysts may also revise forecasts too slowly after earnings surprises, one explanation offered for prices drifting for weeks after results. Negotiators exploit anchoring by opening with an extreme number. A common confusion is mixing anchoring with a reasoned benchmark: comparing price with estimated intrinsic value is analysis; comparing it with an arbitrary past price is anchoring.
example: Say a hypothetical ABC Ltd traded at ₹1,000 last year and now trades at ₹600 after losing its main contract. An anchored investor sees a 40% discount, but if fair value is now ₹450, the stock is still about 33% overvalued (₹600 / ₹450 = 1.33).

short: The habit of seeking out, noticing and believing information that supports what you already think, while ignoring evidence against it.
kid: If you think your team is the best, you remember every goal they score and forget every game they lose. We all like hearing that we are right.
detail: Confirmation bias is the tendency to search for, interpret and remember information in ways that confirm existing beliefs, and to discount or avoid information that contradicts them. Once an investor buys a stock or forms a market view, they may read only bullish reports, follow commentators who agree, and explain away weak results as temporary. This leads to holding flawed positions too long, overconcentration and missed warning signs, and it reinforces overconfidence. Social-media feeds can intensify it by showing people more of what they already engage with. Good practice is to write down an investment thesis along with the specific facts that would prove it wrong, and to actively read the strongest case against it. A common confusion is thinking confirmation bias means deliberately lying to yourself; it usually operates unconsciously, even in careful professional analysts.
example: Say an investor holds a hypothetical PQR Ltd and reads 8 analyst reports on it: 5 positive and 3 negative. He gives full weight to the 5 positive ones and dismisses the rest, so he feels completely sure, even though 3 of 8, or 37.5%, of the reports pointed the other way.

short: Giving too much weight to recent events and assuming they will continue, while paying too little attention to the longer history.
kid: If it rained yesterday and today, you might think it will rain forever. But tomorrow could be sunny. What just happened is not always what comes next.
detail: Recency bias is the tendency to overweight the most recent observations when judging probabilities, and to extend short-term trends into the future. After a strong year, investors pile into last year's best-performing funds or sectors; after a crash, they assume markets will keep falling and avoid equities just when prices are most attractive. Fund-flow data in many markets, including India, show money tends to chase recent performance. It is closely linked to the availability heuristic, since recent events are the easiest to recall. The result is often buying high and selling low. Remedies include studying long-run return and drawdown history, setting a target asset allocation and rebalancing to it on a schedule. A common confusion is with momentum: momentum is a measured effect over specific horizons used in rules-based strategies, whereas recency bias is an unexamined assumption that recent conditions will last.
example: Say a hypothetical sector fund returned 45% last year and an investor moves ₹5 lakh into it expecting the same. If it instead falls 20% the next year, the ₹5 lakh becomes ₹4 lakh, while a diversified fund returning 10% would have grown it to ₹5.5 lakh.

short: The tendency of investors to sell investments that have risen too soon, while holding on to investments that have fallen for too long.
kid: You quickly give away your best, shiniest marble, but keep the cracked one, hoping it will fix itself. Usually, the cracked one stays cracked.
detail: The disposition effect, named by Hersh Shefrin and Meir Statman in 1985, is investors' tendency to realise gains quickly but delay realising losses. It follows from prospect theory and mental accounting: selling a winner brings the pleasure of locking in a gain, while selling a loser forces you to admit a mistake. Terrance Odean's 1998 study of US brokerage accounts found investors were about 50% more likely to sell a winner than a loser, and the winners they sold went on to beat the losers they kept. It can also hurt after-tax returns, because realised losses can usually be set off against taxable gains; in India, capital losses can be set off against capital gains under the Income-tax rules as of 2025, with conditions. A common confusion is with sensible profit-taking: selling is fine when based on valuation, not on whether the position happens to show a gain.
example: Say an investor holds ₹1 lakh each in hypothetical stocks A and B. A rises to ₹1.3 lakh and B falls to ₹70,000. Needing cash, she sells A to lock in its ₹30,000 gain and keeps B to avoid booking its ₹30,000 loss, even though her own research now favours A.

short: The anxious feeling that others are making money from something you are not part of, which pushes people to buy in a rush.
kid: When all your friends are on the swings and you are not, you might run over without thinking. You just do not want to be left out.
detail: Fear of missing out, or FOMO, is the anxiety that others are profiting from an opportunity you have not taken, which pushes people to act quickly and often without proper analysis. In markets it typically appears late in a rally: rising prices, stories of quick gains and social-media chatter draw in buyers who care more about not being left behind than about valuation. It feeds herding and speculative bubbles, as seen in cryptocurrency and meme-stock surges, and in heavily oversubscribed IPOs where some people apply simply because everyone else is. FOMO buying tends to cluster near peaks, so these investors often bear the largest losses when the trend reverses. Defences include a written investment plan, limits on position size and a cooling-off period before acting on tips. A common confusion is mistaking FOMO for conviction: conviction rests on your own analysis, FOMO on other people's gains.
example: Say a hypothetical token rises from $1 to $4 in a month and a friend brags about quadrupling his money. You buy $2,000 worth at $4, getting 500 tokens. If it falls back to $2.50, your holding is worth $1,250, a loss of $750 or 37.5%.

short: The habit of putting money into separate mental buckets, such as salary, bonus or winnings, and treating each differently even though money is interchangeable.
kid: You keep sweets in a red jar and a blue jar. You eat the red-jar sweets freely but save the blue-jar ones, even though they are exactly the same sweets.
detail: Mental accounting, a concept developed by Richard Thaler, describes how people sort money into separate mental accounts based on where it came from or what it is meant for, and then apply different rules to each. Rationally, money is fungible: a rupee from a bonus is worth exactly the same as a rupee from salary. Yet people splurge a tax refund or Diwali bonus, treat stock gains as house money to gamble with, or keep a low-interest savings balance while paying high interest on a credit card. In portfolios, investors may judge each holding separately instead of the whole, which feeds the disposition effect. Mental accounting is not all bad: earmarking money for goals, such as an emergency fund or a child's education, can improve discipline. A common confusion is with budgeting: deliberate budgeting is useful, while mental accounting becomes a bias when it leads to costlier choices.
example: Say you keep ₹1 lakh in a savings account earning 3% a year, labelled 'holiday fund', while carrying a ₹1 lakh credit card balance charged at 36% a year. Keeping both costs ₹36,000 in interest against ₹3,000 earned, a net loss of ₹33,000 a year that clearing the card would avoid.

short: When the same choice leads to different decisions depending on how it is described, for example as a gain versus a loss.
kid: A glass that is half full and a glass that is half empty hold the same water. But saying 'half full' sounds happier, and that can change what we pick.
detail: The framing effect occurs when people make different choices between logically identical options depending on how they are presented. In Tversky and Kahneman's 1981 'Asian disease' experiment, people preferred a sure option when outcomes were framed as lives saved, but a risky option when the same outcomes were framed as lives lost. In finance, a product with a 90% chance of positive returns feels safer than one with a 10% chance of loss; a loan quoting a monthly rate can look cheaper than its annual cost; and investors react differently to daily versus yearly performance figures. Regulators care about framing, which is why disclosure rules standardise formats, such as annualised returns and, in India, SEBI's riskometer for mutual funds. A common confusion is thinking framing changes the facts; it changes only the presentation, which is exactly why it should not change the decision.
example: A loan advertised at '1.5% a month' sounds cheap, but that is 18% a year in simple terms and about 19.56% a year when compounded monthly (1.015^12 = 1.1956). On a ₹1 lakh balance carried for a year, that is roughly ₹19,560 of interest.

short: Judging how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind, so vivid or recent events seem more common than they are.
kid: If you just saw a big dog on TV, you might think big dogs are everywhere. The picture is stuck in your head, so it feels like it happens a lot.
detail: The availability heuristic, described by Tversky and Kahneman in 1973, is the mental shortcut of estimating how frequent or likely something is by how easily examples can be recalled. Events that are recent, dramatic, heavily reported or personally experienced feel more likely than their true base rate. Investors who lived through a crash may overestimate the chance of another and stay out of equities for years, while a stream of stories about stocks that multiplied tenfold or IPOs that soared on listing can make big wins seem routine. Companies that dominate headlines also tend to attract more retail buying regardless of fundamentals, a pattern researchers call attention-driven trading. The bias overlaps with recency bias but is broader, because an old yet vivid memory can also be highly available. A common confusion is thinking it is about access to data; it is about how easily examples come to your own mind.
example: Say the news covers 3 IPOs that doubled on listing day, while 17 others that listed flat or lower get little attention. An investor who remembers only the headlines may think big listing gains are common, though only 3 of 20, or 15%, delivered them.

short: Judging how likely something is by how closely it resembles a familiar type or pattern, while ignoring how common it actually is.
kid: If you see someone in a cape, you might think he is a superhero. But most people in capes are just dressed up for fun. Looking like something does not make it so.
detail: The representativeness heuristic is the shortcut of judging probability by similarity to a stereotype or pattern instead of by statistical reasoning. Tversky and Kahneman showed it leads to base-rate neglect, ignoring how common an outcome is in the first place, and to insensitivity to sample size, reading meaning into short runs of data. In investing, people assume a company with a famous brand, fast sales growth and a charismatic founder must be a good stock, even when its price already reflects all that; or they treat a fund manager's three good years as proof of skill. A useful defence is to start from the base rate, such as how many high-growth newly listed companies actually go on to beat the market, and then adjust for specific evidence. A common confusion is equating a good company with a good investment; the price paid matters as much as the quality.
example: Say 1 in 100 small companies with an exciting story becomes a big long-term winner. A checklist of 'winner traits' spots 90% of future winners but also wrongly flags 10% of the rest. Among 1,000 such companies it flags 9 winners and 99 others, so a flagged company has only about an 8.3% chance (9 / 108) of being a winner, not 90%.
formula: Bayes' rule: P(A given B) = P(B given A) x P(A) / P(B), the correct way to combine a base rate P(A) with new evidence B

short: The mistake of continuing to put money, time or effort into something because of what you have already spent, not because of future benefits.
kid: You built half a sandcastle, but the tide is coming in. Staying to finish it because you already worked so hard just gets you wet.
detail: A sunk cost is money, time or effort already spent that cannot be recovered, whatever you do next. The sunk-cost fallacy is letting those past costs drive future decisions, typically by continuing a failing project or holding a losing investment to avoid 'wasting' what was spent. Rational decisions compare only future costs and benefits, which is why corporate finance excludes sunk costs from capital budgeting and NPV analysis. Examples include a company pouring more money into a plant that will never be profitable, a government extending an unviable project, or an investor buying more of a deteriorating stock purely to lower the average purchase price. The fallacy is closely related to loss aversion and the disposition effect. A common confusion is thinking that walking away wastes the money already spent; that money is gone either way, and only the next decision can still be improved.
example: Say a hypothetical ABC Ltd has spent ₹40 crore on a half-built factory. Finishing it needs another ₹25 crore, and the finished factory is expected to bring in cash worth only ₹20 crore in today's money. Since ₹20 crore is less than ₹25 crore, it should stop, regardless of the ₹40 crore already spent.
formula: Decision rule: continue only if Present value of future benefits > Future costs still to be paid (money already spent is ignored)

short: The tendency to value something more highly simply because you own it, asking more to sell it than you would pay to buy it.
kid: Your old teddy bear may look worn, but you would never swap it, not even for a new one. Things feel more special once they are yours.
detail: The endowment effect, a term coined by Richard Thaler in 1980, is the tendency to place a higher value on something you own than on an identical item you do not. In a 1990 experiment by Daniel Kahneman, Jack Knetsch and Thaler, students given a coffee mug typically asked about twice as much or more to sell it as other students were willing to pay to buy one. It is closely tied to loss aversion, because giving something up feels like a loss. In investing, it shows up as reluctance to sell inherited shares, family property or long-held stocks, and as a preference for leaving a portfolio unchanged even when a better allocation is available. A useful test is to ask whether you would buy the asset today at its current price. A common confusion is equating it with sentimental value; it appears even with ordinary objects owned for minutes.
example: Say you inherit 100 shares of a hypothetical XYZ Ltd worth ₹500 each, or ₹50,000 in all. If you would never spend ₹50,000 of cash to buy those shares today but still refuse to sell them, the endowment effect may be at work.

short: Investors' tendency to hold far more of their own country's shares and bonds than spreading money across the world would suggest.
kid: You always play with the toys in your own room, even though your friends' rooms have great toys too. You stick with what feels familiar.
detail: Home bias is the tendency of investors to put a much larger share of their portfolio into domestic assets than their country's weight in global markets would justify. US investors hold mostly US stocks and Indian investors mostly Indian stocks, even though India makes up only a few percent of world equity market value. Explanations include familiarity, currency risk, better information about local firms, costs and taxes, and regulation; in India, limits on overseas investment, such as the Liberalised Remittance Scheme ceiling for individuals and caps on mutual funds' foreign holdings, also play a role under the rules as of 2025. A related form, local bias, makes people favour nearby companies or their own employer. The cost is weaker diversification, leaving a portfolio exposed to one economy and one currency. A common confusion is assuming any home tilt is irrational; some is justified by local spending needs and costs.
example: Say world equities are worth $100 trillion and a country's market is $5 trillion, or 5% of the total. An investor there with ₹10 lakh entirely in domestic stocks holds 100% at home, compared with about ₹50,000 if her holdings matched world market weights.

short: The mistaken belief that after a run of one outcome, the opposite outcome becomes more likely, even when each event is independent.
kid: If a coin lands on heads five times, you might think tails must come next. But the coin does not remember. Every flip starts fresh.
detail: The gambler's fallacy is the belief that past outcomes of a random, independent process change the odds of the next one, so that a streak must soon 'even out'. Its other name comes from the Monte Carlo Casino in 1913, when a roulette wheel landed on black 26 times in a row and gamblers lost heavily betting on red. In investing, it appears when people assume a stock that has fallen several days running is 'due' for a bounce, or that a crash must be near after several good years, without any reasoning about fundamentals. It stems from the representativeness heuristic: people expect even short sequences to look balanced. It is the mirror image of the hot-hand fallacy, which expects streaks to continue. A common confusion is with mean reversion: genuine mean reversion has an economic cause, such as stretched valuations, whereas coin flips have no memory.
example: A fair coin lands heads 5 times in a row; the chance of that streak was (1/2)^5 = 1/32, about 3.1%. But the chance that the sixth toss is tails is still exactly 50%, because the coin has no memory.
formula: For independent events: P(next outcome given past outcomes) = P(next outcome), e.g. P(tails on toss 6 given 5 heads) = 1/2

short: The belief that a person or investment on a winning streak will keep winning, even when the streak is largely luck.
kid: If your friend wins three races in a row, you might think she will win every race. But maybe she was just lucky on those days.
detail: The hot-hand fallacy is the belief that a run of successes makes further success more likely, even where outcomes are largely independent or driven by chance. The term comes from a 1985 study of basketball shooting by Thomas Gilovich, Robert Vallone and Amos Tversky; later work by Joshua Miller and Adam Sanjurjo (2018) found a statistical flaw in that analysis and evidence of a modest real hot hand, so the lesson is about overrating streaks, not denying they exist. In finance, investors pour money into funds after a few years of top returns, yet S&P Dow Jones Indices' persistence scorecards generally find that few top-quartile funds stay on top. It is the opposite of the gambler's fallacy; both come from misreading randomness. A common confusion is mistaking a short streak for proven skill; separating skill from luck needs long records and risk-adjusted measures.
example: Say 100 hypothetical fund managers each have a 50% chance of beating the market in any year purely by luck. After 3 years, on average 12.5 of them (100 x 0.5^3) will have beaten it every year and look like stars. Each still has only a 50% chance of beating it next year.

short: The tendency, after something happens, to believe you saw it coming all along, making past events seem more predictable than they were.
kid: After you open a present and find a ball, you might say, 'I knew it was a ball!' But before you opened it, you were not sure at all.
detail: Hindsight bias, also called the knew-it-all-along effect, is the tendency to overestimate, once an outcome is known, how predictable it was beforehand. Psychologist Baruch Fischhoff documented it in the 1970s. After a crash such as the 2008 global financial crisis or the March 2020 Covid sell-off, the warning signs look obvious and many people recall having expected it, though few acted on that view at the time. The danger is that it feeds overconfidence: if past events seem predictable, investors assume future ones are too, take bigger bets and judge decisions by outcomes rather than by the quality of the reasoning. It also distorts how fund managers are evaluated. A practical defence is an investment journal that records forecasts and reasons before outcomes are known. A common confusion is treating hindsight bias as learning from experience; real learning compares what you actually predicted with what happened.
example: Say an investor's journal shows that in January she gave a 30% chance to a market fall of 20% or more that year. When the fall happens, she remembers having been almost certain of it. Her written record shows she had in fact put a 70% chance on it not happening.
